The organizers emphasize that partnerships like this demonstrate how collaboration between different institutions can create positive social impact on multiple fronts. With the first batch of shelters complete and already being distributed, the partners plan to continue and expand the initiative in coming months, showing how small acts of craftsmanship can weave together human dignity and animal welfare in unexpectedly beautiful ways.

item.title: What surprised and what went unnoticed: g1 ranks the best shows at João Rock 2026
item.description:
Brazil's João Rock festival returned to Ribeirão Preto with 26 acts across four stages, drawing 65,000 fans to a sold-out celebration of musical diversity. The 2026 edition showcased everything from pop rock to hip hop and reggae, prompting local media outlet G1 to rank the standout performances based on artist delivery, audience reaction, stage presence, and repertoire.
Topping the list was Marina Sena, whose hypnotic performance on the Aquarela stage captivated crowds with a blend of sensuality and mysticism that embodied her recent album "Coisas Naturais." Chico Chico, son of legendary Brazilian rocker Cássia Eller, claimed second place in his festival debut, fearlessly diving into the crowd and delivering a swinging set that honored his roots while carving out his own space in Brazil's new MPB movement. BaianaSystem rounded out the top three with their signature fusion of Afro-rock, dub, and Bahian guitar, accompanied by striking visuals chronicling historical moments from the Cuban Revolution to Brazil's military coup. The Charlie Brown Jr. tribute show proved that nostalgia still packs a punch, transporting fans back to the early 2000s, while Luedji Luna's performance highlighted the power of her voice and her stellar band, blending MPB, jazz, and blues.
This story offers a warm snapshot of Brazil's vibrant music scene, where established artists and emerging talents share stages and generations come together. It's a reminder that festivals can be more than entertainment—they're living archives of culture, history, and the enduring human need to gather and celebrate sound.

item.title: At 64 and with Parkinson's, woman flies on plane and fulfills dream of seeing the sea with adapted wheelchair
item.description:
At 64, Arilda Gonzaga de Assis fulfilled two dreams that once seemed out of reach: flying in an airplane and stepping into the ocean. Living with Parkinson's disease and reduced mobility, she embarked on this journey with the support of her daughters and the help of an amphibious wheelchair provided by lifeguards in Porto Seguro, Brazil. The specially adapted chair, equipped with large air-filled tires that function as floats, allows people with disabilities or limited mobility to safely and comfortably experience the sea.
The trip required careful planning and gentle encouragement. Arilda's family waited until just weeks before departure to tell her about the journey, hoping to avoid unnecessary anxiety. Even then, she nearly backed out, concerned about her physical limitations. But her daughters persisted, reminding her that time doesn't wait and that the experience would be worth facing her fears. At the beach, the amphibious wheelchair made all the difference, enabling Arilda to enter the water safely for the first time in her life.
Arilda's reaction captured the heart of the experience: though she had been afraid of both the ocean and the journey itself, she found the courage to go through with it and emerged transformed. Upon returning home to Campo Grande, she immediately announced she was ready for the next adventure. This quiet story reminds us that accessibility isn't just about infrastructure—it's about creating opportunities for love, joy, and life itself to unfold, regardless of physical limitations.

item.title: ‘I have an understanding housemate’: the student who makes videos of fungus on faeces
item.description:
Alfred Drummond-Herdman has transformed his Edinburgh bedroom into an unlikely laboratory, where wardrobes once filled with clothes now house terrariums of cowpats, grouse droppings, and rabbit pellets. The 27-year-old trainee lawyer photographs fungi emerging from these specimens every 30 seconds, creating mesmerizing time-lapse videos that have captivated millions of viewers worldwide and earned him over 60,000 Instagram followers.
Drummond-Herdman's fascination began during the pandemic, when he encountered cowpats carpeted with mushrooms while walking in Scotland's Ochil Hills. What started as curiosity evolved into serious citizen science: he's now a self-taught taxonomist specializing in coprophilous fungi—those that grow on dung. Working with online forums and experts, he has formally identified two new species, with more discoveries pending. His subjects include vibrantly colored inkcaps, fieldcaps, and the barnacle-like ascobolus, all racing to fruit from the moment herbivore droppings hit the ground. The terrariums don't smell, he notes, because herbivore waste is mostly undigested plants.
This story offers a gentle reminder that extraordinary worlds exist in the most unexpected places. With an estimated 2 million fungi species awaiting discovery globally, Drummond-Herdman's bedroom research represents more than quirky content—it's frontline biodiversity work that makes taxonomy accessible and beautiful. His time-lapses reveal entire lifecycles that would otherwise remain invisible, transforming something most people avoid into windows of wonder. In championing these overlooked organisms, he demonstrates how passion, patience, and a very understanding housemate can illuminate the quiet complexity thriving all around us.

item.title: Beaver dams 'helping boost drought resilience'
item.description:
In a quietly hopeful development for drought-stressed landscapes, beavers are proving to be unexpected allies in building water resilience across England. Dr. Alan Puttock from the University of Exeter has been studying how these industrious mammals—once hunted to extinction in Britain around 400 years ago—are creating complex wetland systems that help landscapes retain water during increasingly common dry spells.
The mechanism is elegantly simple: beaver dams and the ponds they create hold substantial amounts of water and slow its flow into rivers. Puttock's research shows each wetland pond can retain about 1,000 cubic metres of water, reducing peak flows by roughly 30%. During droughts affecting more than half of England, these engineered wetlands provide crucial refuge for struggling wildlife while slowly releasing stored water. Since beavers were reintroduced to Devon's River Otter in 2015, and more recently to Cornwall's Par and Fowey rivers, researchers have observed these benefits firsthand. The wetlands even offer an unexpected bonus: they can act as firebreaks during extreme drought conditions, a concern Puttock admits he hadn't anticipated when he began studying flood management a decade ago.
This story offers a refreshing reminder that sometimes the best solutions to modern environmental challenges come from restoring what was lost. While Puttock is careful to note that beaver wetlands alone won't solve all drought problems, their role as "ecosystem engineers" demonstrates how working with nature—rather than against it—can build landscapes better equipped for both floods and droughts, two extremes of an increasingly unpredictable climate.

item.title: Injured peregrine reunion 'brought tears to eyes'
item.description:
A young peregrine falcon found injured and grounded near a medical centre in Nottingham has been successfully reunited with her family after weeks of rehabilitation. The female bird, discovered at the end of June with injuries preventing flight, received care from two wildlife organizations that nursed her back to health and gave her space to practice flying before her release in late July.
What makes this story particularly touching is the discovery that the injured falcon was the daughter of a male peregrine the same rescue had treated the previous year. Unlike most birds, peregrines don't typically land on the ground when learning to fly—they make short trips and return to the nest. Rescuers suspect she collided with something during her earliest flights. Because the initial shelter lacked facilities for a young bird still developing flight skills, she was transferred to an aviary where she could safely practice. The collaboration between Brinsley Animal Rescue and Leicestershire Wildlife Hospital proved essential to her recovery.
The moment of release offered the kind of quiet magic that wildlife rehabilitation work occasionally delivers. Upon regaining her freedom, the young falcon quickly located her parents and siblings, her calls answered by family members who had been waiting. For the rescuers who had invested weeks of care, watching this reunion unfold was deeply moving—a reminder of why the painstaking work of wildlife rescue matters, and a rare glimpse of a wild family restored to wholeness.
